Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

There is a lot that you can do in the first chapter of Grand Theft Auto 6. You can deep sea dive for treasure, hang out with friends, complete missions, set up for Lucia, and a lot more. However, some of this absolutely needs to be done before you hit the end of the first chapter.

After chapter one, everything in GTA 6 changes, and you don’t have the opportunity to get everything done that you might want to, so you want to be sure that you have a checklist and that you complete it before making your way to Vice City and starting bigger and better things.

Note: It is important to note that taking up Mattia’s offer will end the first chapter of the game. There will also be spoilers ahead about chapter one.

Jason and Lucia have a chance to be madly in love in the beginning of the game. If you prepare for Lucia to get out of prison, work on Jason’s appearance, and focus on how they interact with each other, it will build a solid foundation.

There is a hard reset that comes at the end of the first chapter, and for a while, Lucia will be on her own while Jason recovers. With that being said, it will take a bit of a toll on their relationship.

This means that if you raise it up very high in the beginning, you won’t need to worry about needing to rebuild it as much later in the game, saving you a bit of time later on.

Immediately after setting up your BuckMe account, you are told that you need to start saving money. The first goal in the game is to have a total savings of $5,000 stashed away. This is a pretty easy goal to hit, especially since there are a fair number of money-making opportunities in the first chapter.

You want to make sure that you hit this goal, as when the hard reset comes at the end of the chapter, you will lose everything except what is in your savings account.

As an added bonus, putting money away into your savings account will also raise your relationship, so it is a win-win situation. After you have everything saved up, the rest of your money is stuff you can play with.

Explore the money-making methods covered in this GTA 6 guide, from side activities and selling cars to store robberies and bank heists.

Now that you have saved up the necessary cash for your family savings account, you might have some money burning a hole in your pocket. It is time to go on a bit of a shopping spree.

As I said, you won’t be able to take this money with you into chapter two, so you will want to spend all of it. Buy some clothes, and definitely upgrade your weapons.

There is no point in upgrading your car, as you will lose this after chapter one. Instead, focus on increasing your wardrobe and upgrading your weapons as these will carry over into the next chapter.

There are some missions that you only have access to in the first chapter, and some of them belong to Shirley - Jason’s neighbor. She is a kind lady, and she will occasionally ask you to complete a few tasks.

These consist of getting her some alcohol, and stealing a mobility scooter from a lady nearby. They are fun short missions that you can complete within a few minutes, but they are worth doing because they are quite fun.

Don’t worry about the treasure hunting, as you will be able to come back to it later on. Only certain missions disappear after the first chapter.

A guide to all the story missions in GTA 6 including the chapters and the mission titles.

There’s tons of details in GTA 6, which means that there are a bunch of collectibles that you can find scattered about. Some of these collectibles are books and magazines, and several of them are found around Jason’s house.

Before you end chapter one, you will want to get the books around Jason’s house. These include one in the bedroom, two in the living room, a magazine on the back deck, and one in the shed. Each of these disappears after the first chapter.

Along with this, you will want to grab the sunglasses in Donny’s trailer. You will make your way over there during one of the missions in the first chapter, so you shouldn’t miss out on them, but make sure to pick them up while you have the chance.

If you have been focused on upgrading your weapons, gathering clothes, and putting money into your savings, then you will probably need some extra cash in the first chapter. Instead of searching for treasure, you should instead focus on completing the lost drug missions.

There are four lost drug missions around Key Lento and up to the Grassrivers. These are special missions that end up disappearing after chapter one ends, so you will not have the ability to go back and complete them later on.

Since this is the only time you have access to them, you may as well complete them for the extra cash and spend it on stuff that will help you later in the game.

While I have already established that buying weapons is important because they carry over, it is also important to grab the unique weapons that are obtainable early in the game. There are a couple weapons that you can find around the islands in Key Lento, and they will carry you in later parts of the game.

For instance, the Assassin Pistol can be found on a small dinghy on an island and it is great for completing missions stealthily in later parts of the game, and it has become one of my go-to weapons for staying hidden.

There is also a shotgun that you can find that is quite powerful. It gets outclassed by other unique weapons later on, but it is great to have in chapter two.

One thing that is nice about GTA 6 is that it gives you the option to manually save. This means that you can create save points at key points in the game so that you can return to them later on.

I highly recommend completing what you can in chapter one and then creating a save point right before you go to do the tourist trap mission, as this is the last mission of the chapter, and it is also the point of no return.

If you want to play the game over but don’t want to deal with the slower pacing of the first chapter, you can skip all of that with a save right before the chapter change.

#4212. This dietary supplement may have an unexpected benefit for the brain

A dietary supplement known as urolithin A may help the brain meet its increased demand for oxygen and nutrients during mentally challenging activities. In a clinical trial led by researchers at the University of Oklahoma, middle-aged adults with obesity who took the supplement experienced increased blood flow to the brain while performing a memory task. The findings, published in JAMA Network Open, could shed new light on how urolithin A influences blood vessel function and brain health.

Obesity can affect how blood vessels function, potentially disrupting circulation throughout the body and brain. To investigate whether urolithin A could help counter these effects, the research team recruited 50 adults with obesity between the ages of 40 and 64 for a randomized clinical trial. For four weeks, participants took either 1,000 milligrams of urolithin A each day or a placebo.

Urolithin A Increases Blood Flow to the Brain

During a demanding memory exercise, participants who received urolithin A showed a greater increase in brain blood flow than those in the placebo group. The difference was especially noticeable in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, an area that plays an important role in working memory, the ability to temporarily hold and process information.

However, the researchers observed no significant improvement in blood vessel function in the arm or in participants' performance on memory tests. According to the research team, this is the first study in humans to document an effect of urolithin A on the function of blood vessels in the brain.

"The brain needs an adequate supply of blood to meet the demands of mental activity," said the study's first author, Ana Clara da Costa Pinaffi Langley, Ph.D., an assistant professor in the Department of Nutritional Sciences at the OU College of Allied Health on the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus. "We found that urolithin A increased blood flow to the brain during a memory task, suggesting the supplement may help the brain meet its increased need for oxygen and nutrients when it is working harder. We plan to conduct more research to understand what this finding means for brain health."

A Natural Compound Produced by Gut Bacteria

The human body can produce urolithin A with the help of certain gut bacteria. These microorganisms generate the substance by breaking down naturally occurring compounds in foods such as pomegranates, strawberries, and walnuts.

Not everyone produces the same amount of urolithin A. Previous research suggests that the ability to generate the compound naturally tends to diminish as people grow older and their body mass index increases, Langley explained. Urolithin A can also be obtained directly through dietary supplements.

Participants tolerated the supplement well throughout the trial. However, the researchers cautioned that the study involved a relatively small number of people at a single research site. Larger, longer clinical trials will be necessary to better understand the supplement's effects.

Could Urolithin A Support Healthier Brain Aging?

Although the increase in brain blood flow is encouraging, it remains unclear whether this change could translate into lasting improvements in cognitive health.

"These findings offer an interesting starting point for understanding how urolithin A affects the brain," said study co-author Andriy Yabluchanskiy, M.D., Ph.D., an associate professor in the Department of Neurosurgery at the OU College of Medicine. "Although we saw increased blood flow to the brain during mental activity, participants did not demonstrate measurable improvements in memory or attention. Future studies will need to determine whether taking the supplement for a longer period leads to meaningful improvements in cognitive function or other health benefits."

For Langley, the broader aim is to extend healthspan, the portion of a person's life spent in good health.

"The idea is to mitigate cognitive decline," she said. "We want to expand the time that people are living healthier lives."

Materials provided by University of Oklahoma. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4209. Tomorrow's Battlefield 6 patch somehow makes jets more useless, improves armor bar visibility in Redsec

The first Battlefield 6 patch of the year is almost here, bringing a smattering of changes, including one that doesn't quite make sense.

Battlefield 6’s promised, season-extending update has been officially detailed. The patch, version 1.1.3.5, arrives tomorrow, January 20 right when Season 1 was supposed to end. Part of the update’s goal is to extend the current season, until Season 2 kicks off in the middle of February.

Update 1.1.3.5 does, of course, have a change log of its own that goes beyond just the season’s extension, but the changes fall somewhere between not very exciting, and a bit puzzling.

Patch 1.1.3.5 is, for all intents and purposes, a smaller update. When Battlefield Studios announced it earlier last week, the developer didn’t promise any major changes or fixes, so expectations never got out of hand.

The patch is mainly made up of bug fixes, but it does have three key areas of improvements to gameplay. There’s a big focus on melee combat, how responsive/unresponsive it is with the various melee tools, and how melee behaviour interacts with sprinting and other animations.

The end result should be faster attack speeds for the knife, and clearer wind-up animations for both the knife and the sledgehammer. The timing dictating when melee damage gets credited has also been made more consistent in different environments.

Interestingly, sprint is now only interrupted when the melee attack reaches its target. As it stands, sprinting is only interrupted after the full duration of the animation has been completed, which adds to the that perceived feeling of sluggishness.

The other major, and arguably most confusing is the nerf to jet cannons. The patch is going to make jets far less stronger against other air vehicles, requiring 40% more hits to destroy a target. This is puzzling because jets - and air vehicles in general - are already the least survivable in Battlefield 6.

And, considering how the rest of a jet's arsenal is either situational or nearly ineffective, the cannons were really the one guaranteed way of downing other air vehicles, so long as you manage to land your shots consistently. While the change is wellmeaning, the percentage will likely be reduced in future patches.

Finally, the update makes a few refinements to UI across the game, though mainly aimed at Redsec and modes where players wear armor. Armor bar visibility has been improved, and there’s a fix for the annoying bug that sometimes caused the armor bar to disappear every few seconds.

Panini America announced its partnership with Rockstar Games on November 24. The officially licensed set is called the GTA VI: Sports Trading Card Collection, and it'll be the first trading card collaboration between the two companies.

Even if you don't care about the numbered cards, there's some appeal in having the regular ones. GTA's fictional athletes aren't exactly household names like the ones you'd find in Panini's other sports collections, but you can actually go looking for their cards in Leonida while playing the game.

Rockstar has been selling GTA merchandise for years, but this particular collaboration reminds me of the sort of extras that used to come with physical copies of video games. The maps that came with older GTA titles, for instance, were something you could actually use while playing and keep long after you were done with the game.

Ironically, GTA 6's boxed edition doesn't even come with a game disc. So it's nice to see Rockstar making something physical that draws directly from the game rather than simply putting its logo on another piece of merchandise.

Rockstar could've easily gone with a conventional trading card set featuring Jason, Lucia, and other major characters. Instead, it's making replicas of things you might stumble across while taking a break from the story. I'd love to see Rockstar do something similar with other fictional brands from the series, like Sprunk or eCola.

Unfortunately, Panini hasn't announced an exact release date, pricing, or which countries the cards will be available in.

Depending on when the cards go on sale in December, they could make for a pretty good Christmas gift for a GTA fan.

#4207. Common supplements rival antibiotics in treating severe gum disease

A familiar dietary supplement combined with low-dose aspirin may offer an unexpected alternative to antibiotics for people with severe gum disease. In a year-long clinical trial, patients who received omega-3 and aspirin alongside conventional periodontal treatment experienced nearly identical clinical benefits to those who received antibiotics. Perhaps even more surprisingly, the improvements were still evident six months after supplementation ended.

The findings, published in the Journal of Periodontology, come from researchers affiliated with Albert Einstein Israelite Hospital, Guarulhos University (UNG), the University of Taubaté (UNITAU), and the Ribeirão Preto School of Dentistry at USP (FORP-USP) in Brazil, as well as Harvard University in the United States.

The study suggests that combining omega-3 with low-dose acetylsalicylic acid (ASA), better known as aspirin, could reduce the need for antibiotics in certain patients. The discovery is particularly timely given growing worldwide concerns about antibiotic resistance, which occurs when bacteria develop the ability to survive exposure to drugs designed to kill them.

Why Severe Gum Disease Is So Difficult To Treat

Researchers monitored 109 patients with advanced periodontitis over 12 months. Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease that develops when bacteria accumulate below the gumline, triggering an immune response that can gradually damage the tissues and bone that hold teeth in place. Without proper treatment, the disease can cause teeth to loosen and eventually fall out.

As periodontitis progresses, spaces known as periodontal pockets form between the teeth and gums. These pockets can become increasingly deep, making it difficult to remove harmful bacteria through ordinary brushing and flossing.

"Patients with severe disease have very deep pockets, which act as reservoirs for bacteria associated with the disease. It's a very challenging condition to treat," says dental surgeon Nídia Cristina Castro dos Santos, the first author of the study and a professor and researcher at Einstein.

The researchers randomly divided the participants into four treatment groups. Every patient received subgingival instrumentation, commonly referred to as scaling. This standard periodontal treatment involves removing bacterial deposits and hardened plaque from tooth surfaces beneath the gums. Each group also received a different complementary treatment.

Patients in the control group received inactive substitutes for the antibiotics, omega-3, and aspirin, supplied in capsules that looked identical to those containing the active treatments.

A second group received metronidazole and amoxicillin three times daily for 14 days. This combination of antibiotics has some of the strongest scientific evidence supporting its use as an additional treatment for severe periodontitis.

Participants in the third group took three grams of omega-3 each day, together with a daily dose of low-dose aspirin, for six months. The fourth group received both interventions, taking antibiotics for two weeks while following the six-month omega-3 and aspirin regimen.

The researchers assessed the patients' progress at three, six, and 12 months.

At the end of the study, approximately 58% of patients in the antibiotic group had reached the researchers' clinical treatment target, defined as having no more than four remaining deep periodontal pockets.

The omega-3 and aspirin group achieved an almost identical success rate of 57.7%. By comparison, only 23.1% of patients who underwent scaling and received placebos reached the same target. Interestingly, administering both antibiotics and the omega-3 and aspirin regimen together did not produce any additional benefits.

Although antibiotics can improve treatment outcomes in patients with particularly severe gum disease, they are not routinely necessary for everyone with periodontitis.

"The use of antibiotics isn't considered the gold standard of treatment. Although metronidazole and amoxicillin yield good results in the most severe cases, their use should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis due to risks related to bacterial resistance and possible adverse effects," says Castro dos Santos.

Helping the Body Naturally Resolve Inflammation

The findings build on earlier research into the potential role of omega-3 fatty acids in protecting oral health. In a previous investigation, also supported by FAPESP and published in Scientific Reports, scientists found that omega-3 supplementation reduced periodontal inflammation and bone loss in rats. The protective effects were particularly notable when supplementation was combined with physical exercise.

Although results from animal studies do not necessarily translate directly to humans, the earlier findings provided clues that omega-3 might help regulate the inflammatory processes that contribute to gum disease.

Omega-3 fatty acids are a group of fats found in foods such as oily fish and are widely available as dietary supplements. Beyond their nutritional importance, they serve as building blocks for certain molecules that help regulate inflammation.

Castro explains that omega-3 works differently from conventional anti-inflammatory medications. Instead of simply interfering with pathways that promote inflammation, omega-3 helps the body produce molecules involved in bringing inflammation to a natural conclusion and supporting tissue repair.

This process, known as the resolution of inflammation, is an active biological mechanism that helps the body return to normal after an immune response. In chronic inflammatory diseases such as periodontitis, inflammation can persist and contribute to ongoing tissue damage.

The researchers included low-dose aspirin because it can promote the formation of certain inflammation-resolving molecules. They suspected that combining aspirin with omega-3 could strengthen the body's ability to control the persistent inflammation associated with advanced gum disease.

The researchers had originally expected antibiotics and the omega-3 regimen to work best when administered together. Instead, the findings revealed that targeting inflammation could produce clinical improvements comparable to those achieved through antibiotic treatment.

"We imagined that the combination of antibiotics and omega-3 would be most effective in controlling periodontitis in these patients. We also believed that the results for the group that used omega-3 with ASA would be slightly lower than those for the antibiotic group. The result was surprising because the two therapies performed very similarly, paving the way for it to become a treatment option for these patients," says Castro.

Equally intriguing was how long the improvements lasted. Six months after patients stopped taking omega-3 and aspirin, their clinical outcomes remained similar to those observed when the treatment ended.

According to Castro, this persistence raises the possibility that adjusting the body's inflammatory response could have lasting therapeutic effects. However, scientists are still working to understand the biological mechanisms responsible.

A Potential Alternative Amid Rising Antibiotic Resistance

For dental surgeon Magda Feres, the study's lead author and a full professor at the Harvard School of Dental Medicine and the Graduate Program in Dentistry at UNG, targeting the body's inflammatory response could provide a valuable treatment option for certain patients.

"The combination of omega-3 and low-dose aspirin achieved clinical benefits comparable to those of the metronidazole and amoxicillin protocol, opening up a real alternative for those who can't take antibiotics, especially patients with allergies or intolerance to these medications," she says.

The potential to reduce antibiotic use has implications that extend well beyond dentistry. Antibiotic resistance ranks among the greatest threats to global public health, making it increasingly important to identify effective treatment strategies that do not depend on these medications.

"Demonstrating that it's possible to treat severe periodontitis by modulating the body's own response is new and relevant information that helps preserve antibiotics for when they are truly indispensable," says Feres.

More Research Is Needed Before Clinical Practice Changes

Despite the encouraging findings, the researchers caution that the results are not sufficient to justify an immediate change in how dentists treat severe periodontitis. The participants did not have other significant systemic or oral diseases, meaning the results may not apply equally to patients with additional health conditions.

Larger studies involving more diverse populations will be needed to validate the findings and determine which patients are most likely to benefit from each treatment strategy.

It is also important to recognize that omega-3 and aspirin were used alongside professional periodontal treatment, rather than as a substitute for it. Aspirin carries potential risks, including an increased risk of bleeding, and may not be appropriate for everyone.

Meanwhile, Feres and her colleagues are investigating how the different treatments affect the communities of bacteria living inside periodontal pockets. Early microbiological findings point to a decline in bacterial species associated with periodontal disease and an increase in microorganisms linked to healthier gums.

These ongoing investigations could help explain why targeting inflammation produced such promising results and whether the approach can reliably benefit a broader range of patients.

"It's an important step forward, but not the end of the story. Therefore, the message is one of cautious optimism: we have a promising, scientifically plausible alternative to antibiotics in select cases. Routine replacement will require more evidence," she concludes.

#4206. A fat-burning molecule has an unexpected benefit for your muscles

Researchers have identified a naturally occurring molecule that plays a crucial role in building muscle strength and improving physical performance. Released during exercise, the molecule could also provide the basis for future treatments to protect against muscle damage associated with type 2 diabetes.

The molecule, known as L-β-aminoisobutyric acid (L-BAIBA), is essential for muscles to adapt to physical activity. It helps muscles become stronger, improves their resistance to fatigue, and protects against damage and weakness.

The study, published in Nature Communications and funded by Diabetes UK and the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC), reveals that L-BAIBA is a central regulator of the biological changes that allow muscles to improve their strength, structure, and endurance in response to exercise training.

How Exercise Triggers a Natural Muscle Booster

Although the health benefits of exercise are well established, scientists still do not fully understand the biological processes that allow the body to adapt to physical demands. A research team led by Professor Lee Roberts at the University of Leeds investigated whether these processes could reveal new ways to treat chronic conditions such as type 2 diabetes.

L-BAIBA has attracted scientific interest for more than a decade. In research published in 2014, Roberts demonstrated that the molecule has beneficial effects on metabolism, helping to enhance the body's ability to burn fat in response to exercise. L-BAIBA is now commercially available as a dietary supplement.

The latest findings reveal another important function of the molecule. L-BAIBA acts as a chemical messenger that connects physical activity with beneficial changes in muscle structure and metabolism, helping muscles adapt to the demands placed on them.

Lee Roberts, Professor of Molecular Physiology and Metabolism at the University of Leeds, said: "Our research identifies L-BAIBA as an exercise-induced signal that helps muscles adapt, improve their metabolic capacity and ability to contract, and ultimately enhances physical performance.

"This gives us exciting new insight into how exercise benefits the body and highlights a promising target for future therapies aimed at preserving muscle function in chronic conditions such as diabetes."

Protecting Muscles Against Damage From Type 2 Diabetes

The researchers also discovered that L-BAIBA protects muscles against damage associated with type 2 diabetes. The condition can negatively affect muscle health, leading to a decline in muscle mass and strength, as well as disruptions in the way muscles process and use energy. These complications can significantly reduce a person's quality of life.

Because regular physical activity is an important part of managing type 2 diabetes, finding ways to improve muscle function and reduce fatigue could make a substantial difference for people who struggle to exercise.

Type 2 diabetes is a serious chronic condition that increases the risk of potentially life-threatening complications, including heart attacks and strokes. Its development is influenced by a complex combination of factors, including age, ethnicity, genetics, and living with overweight or obesity.

Although type 2 diabetes has traditionally been more common among older adults, diagnoses in people younger than 40 have been rising in recent years. Cases in this younger age group are now increasing more rapidly than among adults over 40.

A Promising Target for Future Diabetes Treatments

Anna Morris, Assistant Director of Research Strategy and Partnership at Diabetes UK, said: "Exercise plays an important role in managing type 2 diabetes, but for many people muscle weakness and fatigue can make staying active a real challenge. This research helps us better understand how muscles adapt to exercise and identifies a potential new target for improving muscle health. While these findings are still at an early stage, they could help shape future approaches that support people with type 2 diabetes to remain active and live healthier, longer lives."

Although the discovery opens promising avenues for future treatments, further research is needed to determine whether L-BAIBA supplementation can produce meaningful therapeutic benefits in people with type 2 diabetes.

The research was led by the University of Leeds in collaboration with:

The study was funded by Diabetes UK and BBSRC.

#4204. Harvard’s tiny UV light chip could help shrink quantum computers

Ultraviolet (UV) light is already essential to a wide range of modern technologies. Beyond its natural presence in sunlight, it is used to disinfect surfaces, make biological materials fluoresce, and manufacture computer chips through a process called photolithography. In the future, microscopic sources of UV light built directly into photonic chips could enable smaller quantum computers, ultra-precise atomic clocks, and other advanced technologies.

However, shrinking UV light sources to fit on a chip has presented a significant engineering challenge. Ultraviolet light rapidly loses power as it travels through optical waveguides, the tiny channels that carry light across a chip. This limitation has made it extremely difficult to develop compact UV sources with enough power for practical applications.

Now, a Harvard-led research team has demonstrated a microscopic photonic device that produces approximately 120 times more UV power than previous comparable devices. The researchers, working in the laboratory of Marko Lončar, the Tiantsai Lin Professor of Electrical Engineering, achieved the breakthrough using a widely studied material called thin-film lithium niobate.

Published in Nature Communications, the findings establish lithium niobate as a promising platform for generating powerful ultraviolet light in compact devices while minimizing optical losses.

Rather than trying to deliver ultraviolet light directly through microscopic channels, the researchers designed a device that generates UV light from red light within the chip itself.

The approach relies on a process known as frequency upconversion. Inside the lithium niobate crystal, two photons of red light combine to produce a single ultraviolet photon with higher energy. Lithium niobate is particularly well suited to this process because of its exceptional ability to convert light from one frequency to another.

"Our group is perhaps best known for utilizing lithium niobate for photonic devices that operate at longer, infrared wavelengths -- closer to the realm of telecommunications signals," Lončar said.

However, the team found that this transparent crystalline material, which has become increasingly important in integrated photonics, can also support light sources and guide light at much shorter wavelengths, including those in the ultraviolet range.

"When people think about [thin-film lithium niobate], they don't think of it as a UV material, but we show that it is," said co-first author Kees Franken, former research fellow in the Lončar lab. "We also show that there are some other nonlinear effects happening that we don't fully understand yet."

A New Technique Overcomes a Major Engineering Barrier

The device uses optical waveguides, microscopic channels etched into the lithium niobate film that direct light through the chip in much the same way electrical wires carry current.

For red light to be efficiently converted into ultraviolet light, the orientation of regions within the crystal must be repeatedly reversed at precisely controlled intervals along the waveguide. This manufacturing process, called poling, is a specialized technique used in nonlinear optics.

One of the biggest challenges has been creating these patterns with accuracy at scales smaller than a micrometer across devices that extend for centimeters.

Previous manufacturing methods required researchers to make an undesirable compromise. Poling the entire film before forming the waveguides made it difficult to correct manufacturing imperfections. Alternatively, creating the waveguides first reduced conversion efficiency because the electrodes were positioned too far away, allowing only part of the film to be successfully poled.

To eliminate this tradeoff, the Harvard team developed a technique they call "sidewall poling."

Precision Engineering Dramatically Improves Light Conversion

Instead of positioning the electrodes exclusively above the lithium niobate film, the researchers placed precisely patterned metal structures resembling tiny fingers directly alongside the etched waveguide. During fabrication, they applied a small voltage to permanently reverse the orientation of the crystal domains in a carefully controlled pattern.

"The key idea was: could we just put the electrodes directly on the waveguide?" said co-first author and former graduate student Soumya Ghosh. "It's a high-precision fabrication process to position the electrodes but requiring about 50-nanometer accuracy."

This arrangement enabled the researchers to reverse the crystal domains throughout the entire cross section of the waveguide, allowing light traveling through the material to undergo much more efficient frequency conversion.

The team could also fine-tune the spacing of the reversed crystal regions along the device. By incorporating existing "adapted poling" techniques previously developed in Lončar's laboratory and elsewhere, the researchers compensated for variations in the thickness of the lithium niobate film and the shape of the waveguide.

The resulting device generated 4.2 milliwatts of ultraviolet power directly on the chip at a wavelength of 390 nanometers. That represents approximately 120 times the output power achieved by the best previous thin-film lithium niobate devices operating in this wavelength range.

Earlier experiments using the material generated only tens of microwatts of UV power. Although those results demonstrated that the approach was scientifically feasible, the output was too low to support practical applications.

The substantial increase in power could be particularly valuable for trapped-ion quantum computers. These machines use electrically charged atoms to store and process quantum information. Many of the specific atomic energy transitions required to operate them involve light in the near-ultraviolet portion of the spectrum.

"If you want a scalable quantum computer that isn't the size of a truck, you need to scale everything down to the chip level, and this includes the light sources," Franken said.

The technology could also benefit ultra-precise atomic clocks and environmental monitoring systems. According to the researchers, the same range of ultraviolet wavelengths is well suited to compact sensors designed to closely monitor greenhouse gases and other atmospheric pollutants.

Franken and Ghosh attribute the breakthrough partly to the collaborative structure of Lončar's laboratory, where researchers carry out every stage of device development in one place, including theoretical research, engineering design, cleanroom fabrication, and optical testing.

"The hands-on intuition that we gained for how to make a device, while also keeping the zoomed-out view of what this device is for, and how we were going to characterize it -- that's a big part of what enabled this project for us," Ghosh said.

"Milliwatt-level UV generation using sidewall poled lithium niobate" was further co-authored by C.C. Rodrigues, J. Yang, C.J. Xin, S. Lu, D. Witt, G. Joe, G.S. Wiederhecker, and K.-J. Boller.

U.S. federal funding for the project came from the following sources: Department of the Air Force grant No. FA9453-23-C-A039; Office of Naval Research grant No. N00014-22-C-1041/VAS-21-0001; NASA grant No. 80NSSC22K0262 and 80NSSC23PB442; and National Science Foundation grants ERC EEC-1941583 and OMA-2137723.

#4203. Heartopia surprise launches on Steam and shockingly, everyone seems to be happy

Heartopia players didn't actually end up having to wait too long to play the game on Steam, which is certainly not what anyone expected.

Heartopia has officially arrived on Steam, only a little over a week after it launched on iOS and Android. When the game’s release date was announced back in December, developer XD said it was pushing back the Steam release without offering any hints about how long the delay was going to be.

While the game can be played on PC through TapTap, the developer’s own emulator, many had been anticipating the Steam launch. So you can imagine that when the free-to-play life sim game surprisingly showed up on Valve’s platform on Saturday, there were a lot of happy people.

Heartopia’s Steam release has, much like mobile launch, been a success. We do know that the game reached the number one spot across app stores in over 50 countries, and though the Steam numbers may not be as record-breaking, everything is looking pretty good.

The game peaked at a decent 28,815 concurrent players (via SteamDB) on Steam one day after it launched, and considering how sticky it has been with the majority of those players so far - and the fact the launch itself was a surprise - there’s every chance those figures will improve over the course of this week as it picks up momentum.

Steam user reviews have similarly been quite positive, with the overall rating currently sitting at Mostly Positive, based on over 1,400 reviews.

You’re still need either a Google, Facebook, or Apple account to log into the game, same as you would on mobile. The Steam version does support cross-play with other platforms, so you’ll be able to play with your friends on mobile.

We’ve been playing a lot of Heartopia ourselves, and have been updating and expanding our guides. If you’re looking to get started, such as with how to add and play with friends, how to regain Energy, and how to unlock home plots, our guides offer the best place to start.

No Org No Problem won the opening and deciding maps against Stallions Esports to reach the MENA Qualifier Playoffs grand final. One more series win against Mix My Miks would send them to VCT EMEA Kickoff 2027 in Berlin alongside partner teams including Fnatic.

Against Stallions Esports, the semi-final went the full distance. No Org No Problem took the opening map in 48 minutes. Stallions Esports levelled on the second, winning a 54-minute contest. No Org No Problem then closed out the decider in 43 minutes.

Stallions Esports won Middle East Qualifier 2 from 16 to 18 November, ahead of Mayhem. Mix My Miks won North Africa Qualifier 1, a single-elimination event from 9 to 11 November, ahead of BAAM Esports. Each of those qualifiers had 64 teams.

Mix My Miks booked their final place by beating Gamax Esports in the second semi-final. That match also went to three maps. The four-team playoffs are being played online in a single-elimination bracket. The semi-finals were best of three.

Fnatic were confirmed in October 2026 as staying on as a VCT EMEA partner for 2027.

The tournament will be played in person at the Riot Games Arena in Berlin in early 2027. For the MENA winner, the trip carries direct financial value. Riot’s support for non-partner teams starts at Kickoff, and the sums rise for teams that progress further through the season.

Non-partner teams that qualify for Masters receive US$200,000, and those reaching Champions receive US$400,000, Dot Esports reported. Europe’s route to Kickoff runs in parallel. #4201. Marathon’s Symbiosis Update Adds Host Of New Modes, Including Permanent PvE, Next Month

Bungie has detailed its upcoming Symbiosis update for Marathon, which introduces several significant modes next month. Chief among them is the new permanent PvE mode, which Bungie previously experimented with and promised earlier this year.

Symbiosis is headlined by Expedition, a co-op PvE destination with roguelite elements. Expedition pits teams of players against escalating challenges and offers randomized upgrades called Flash Boosts to increase their odds of success.

The Perimeter zone has also been expanded with the new Burrows and Reservoir areas. Another addition is Limbo, a new social hub for players to gather that features a firing range. You can also try out the new sword-wielding Bishop Runner Shell alongside new weapons and gear, such as the Maverick pistol, throwing knife, hack grenade, and V17 flamethrower. Lastly, you can test your skills against other players in the beta PvP Deathmatch mode.

Symbiosis arrives in Marathon on December 8. An open play week will kick off the same day, allowing new players to experience all of Marathon’s content for free until December 15.

The Symbiosis update marks Marathon's evolution into a more co-op-friendly, PvE experience as its initial focus on PvP extraction has struggled to sustain a substantial audience since its March 5 launch. Bungie announced in September that it plans to spend the rest of 2026 improving Marathon's core mechanics and features while giving players more agency for how they engage with it beyond competitive PvP.

#4200. Battlefield 6’s first big map in months is coming to Labs soon, but I'm more excited about BF4's Golmud Railway making its way to BF6

As promised, Battlefield Labs is coming back to bring us a preview of some of Battlefield 6’s upcoming Season 2 content.

Battlefield 6’s Season 2 was recently pushed back by a month to give Battlefield Studios time to polish up its content. Now, the developer has revealed how it plans to use some of that time, and the first port of call is Battlefield Labs.

As discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content. This includes Season 2, of course, and a big component of what it’s bringing to the game is headed to Labs.

The first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the new maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2. BF Studios says the map falls between Eastwood and Mirak Valley, in terms of size.

The blog post even likened it to Battlefield 1’s St. Quentin Scar, and Battlefield 5’s Arras. Although we’ve yet to actually play it, the size and description do sound really well, especially in a game as starved of big maps as Battlefield 6 currently is.

Another thing BF Studios wants to test is the way ground vehicle gameplay and aerial presence interact with infantry combat, which is pretty standard for most Battlefield maps. Interestingly, there appears to be some sort of mechanic unique to Contaminated that the developer also wants to evaluate.

More Labs sessions are planned, including one that will show off new gameplay tools and vehicles. The AH-6 Little Bird helicopter was specifically namedropped, which makes sense given that it’s going to be part of Season 2’s content.

Battlefield Labs sessions will also extend beyond the biggest-ticket items of maps and vehicles. BF Studios said we should expect tests of upcoming features, like the Aircraft Radar, as part of a list of other air combat updates.

Ground vehicles, and they way the various rockets interact with them, will also be evaluated in a different session, with specific adjustments planned for RPGs and TOWs. And, of course, the work to improve and perfect hit reg remains ongoing, and future tweaks will go through Labs first.

There’s even more exciting news for fans of big maps, as the blog post also confirmed that Battlefield 4’s Golmud Railway is currently in the works, planned to go live in a future season. Golmud Railway will show up early in Labs, and you can expect it to evolve over multiple sessions.

For context, when it does arrive in Battlefield 6, Golmud Railway will be the largest map in the game, which is saying something. Though the map is beloved by vehicle players, it has its issues elsewhere, and BF Studios says it will be looking at all that when it creates the BF6, emphasising that it won’t be a simple port of the BF4 original.

Finally, the post throws a bone to Redsec battle royale players still waiting for a Solo mode. BF Studios continues to test the idea internally, but it’s taking a while. Needless to say, there are so many aspects that need to be considered. Game pace, balance, player survivability, match flow just to name a few.

Redsec BR was built with squads in mind, so that task is extra challenging. Though the developer didn’t say when we can expect Solos to arrive in Labs, players will get a chance to experience it before it enters the live game.

#4199. Take-Two's GTA 6 PC Port Crackdown Has Already Taken Down Over 3,000 Repositories

Grand Theft Auto 6 is still a console exclusive, but some fans have already been trying to get it running on PC. Take-Two Interactive has filed a copyright complaint against Leonida, an unofficial port based on the Xbox Series version of the game. It's not just the original project that's been affected: GitHub has taken action against a whopping 3,007 repositories in response to the complaint.

According to a new rumor, Rockstar Games could release the GTA 6 PC port just a few months after the highly anticipated console launch.

Leonida was named after the fictional state in which GTA 6 takes place, and it was one of several attempts to get the console version running on a computer. Unlike some of the fan-made PC ports we've seen for older console games, though, this one was being developed using a build of a game that had only just come out.

In a DMCA notice published on GitHub on November 24, Take-Two's intellectual property enforcement team alleges that Leonida infringes upon the company's copyright and violates Rockstar's terms of service. The notice says an Xbox Series build of GTA 6 was leaked on November 20, with the Leonida repository appearing a day later.

The developers had asked users to supply their own game files, but Take-Two argues that the project was designed specifically to make use of the leaked build. The company requested that GitHub take down Leonida and its forks, arguing that the alleged infringement couldn't be addressed without disabling the repositories altogether.

GitHub says it acted on the entire network of 3,007 repositories. That number includes forks, which are essentially copies of a repository that other GitHub users can work on independently. That doesn't mean there were 3,007 different GTA 6 PC ports in development, though.

An Xbox Series build of GTA 6 was leaked on November 20, with the Leonida repository appearing a day later.

According to PC Gamer, the team appeared to have reached the game's splash screen during a livestream before it crashed. The project's lead developer, NotRexed, subsequently announced their departure, citing the loss of the Discord server as well as the pressure of managing the community alongside school and sports.

Take-Two's takedown hasn't put an end to Leonida, either. According to the same report, others have already tried to pick up where the original developer left off.

It's a familiar situation for those of us who primarily play on PC. GTA 4 came to PC several months after its console debut, while we had to wait more than a year and a half after GTA 5's original launch for its PC version. Even Red Dead Redemption 2 took roughly a year to make its way over.

The difference this time is that a report has suggested GTA 6 could arrive on PC in the first quarter of 2027. If that turns out to be true, the wait would be much shorter than it was for Rockstar's last two major releases. There hasn't been an official announcement confirming that release window, however.

Getting GTA 6 to boot on a PC and getting it to run well enough to play through the entire game are two very different things. Just look at how badly Rockstar handled GTA 4's PC port. Even hardware that far exceeded the game's original system requirements struggled to run it smoothly, and Rockstar never bothered to properly fix it.

Modders have spent years ironing out its performance issues and bugs, and while that's still an ongoing process, I'd argue 2026 has been the best year yet to play GTA 4 on PC. Even if one of these unofficial efforts eventually makes it past the splash screen, there's no telling how well the game will run on a typical gaming PC or whether it'll have major bugs throughout the story.

Hopefully, Rockstar won't keep us in the dark for too long regarding the official PC version. Even an approximate release window would be welcome at this point, especially for anyone holding off on buying a console just to play GTA 6.

That's not shocking – GTA VI is, by many metrics, the most anticipated game in history, with its predecessor, Grand Theft Auto V, selling nearly 235 million copies since its launch back in 2013. There's also the fact that Rockstar Games is not releasing a physical edition of GTA VI, per se. Yes, you can go to a store to pick up a GTA VI box (and you can do so today, allowing you to preload the game), but inside that box will be a download code for a digital version of the game – you won't find GTA VI on a physical disc. So, naturally, many players are opting to purchase the game on digital storefronts like the PlayStation and Xbox game stores.

"Grand Theft Auto VI, the most preordered title of all time on the Microsoft Store, launches November 19," an Xbox blog post reads. "Considering the unprecedented demand, we encourage everyone to begin preloading as soon as possible to ensure you're prepared for launch day." PlayStation echoes this statement with a blog post of its own that reads, "Grand Theft Auto VI is now the most preordered game in the history of the PlayStation Store. Given this unprecedented demand, we've joined with Rockstar Games to allow players to start preloading the game nine days early, so they're ready to play on launch day."

There you have it: People are very excited about Grand Theft Auto VI.

Grand Theft Auto VI launches next week on November 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S.

#4197. Arc Raiders finally reveals early 2026 roadmap, but we’re not getting a new map for a while

The first couple of months of 2026 in the world of Arc Raiders look pretty promising, but the big guns are being held back for now.

After weeks of waiting, Arc Raiders developer Embark has officially unveiled the first few months of the game’s 2026 roadmap. The plan is split into four months, covering January to April, collectively dubbed Escalation.

We’re expecting a content update each month, with the majority of the biggest additions happening on the game’s existing maps. There is, however, at least one new map in the works, but it won’t be here until sometime in April.

While we wait for that, Arc Raiders is going to go through several events and other in-game changes, some more meaningful (and exciting) than others. January looks to be the lightest so far, which makes sense given that it’s just a week or so from ending.

January’s chapter is titled Headwinds, kicking off on January 27. This segment will see the addition of a new matchmaking option for players above level 40 - at or near the game’s endgame. We’re also expecting a new Map Condition, and a new Player Project for everyone to contribute to.

Things start getting interesting in February, when Shrouded Sky will begin. This chapter brings three exciting additions to Arc Raiders. There will be a new Map Condition, new Arc Threat, and the start of another Player Project.

Interestingly, we’re going to see some sort of map update during the month, but Embark didn’t share anymore details. The next Raider Deck will also deploy in February, alongside a new Expedition Window.

The Flashpoint chapter begins in March, when we’re expecting another new Map Condition, one more new Arc Threat, as well as another Player Project. March’s most interesting addition is an update to everyone’s trusty rooster friend, Scrappy.

Finally, April is when the big guns come out, because that’s when the first new map of 2026 will arrive in Arc Raiders. With it, comes a new large Arc, which is to be expected. A new Map Condition will debut then, too, likely starting off on the new map.

That’s pretty much it, but seeing as we’re just one day away from the start of the January stage, things are about to get exciting again in Arc Raiders.

#4196. Australia Did It: End-of-the-World Railway Defense Business Review - Delivering Where It Matters

Australia Did It: End-of-the-world Railway Defense Business is a game I catch myself playing in my head long after I shut it off. Though it uses turn-based strategy as its base, it expands beyond the genre’s regular confines, blending elements from roguelikes, puzzle games, bullet-heaven titles, and the tower-defense genre. The result is an experience that demands wide-scale experimentation and rewards improvisation.

In a post-apocalyptic world where the Atlantic Ocean has dried up, you risk your life to ensure your shipment reaches its destination. Riding from station to station by train, you must build your team amid your many missions as various mutated creatures, malicious machines, and coordinated soldiers attack your convoy. Lore is doled out piecemeal and serves mostly as background dressing, but each time I learned more about the world, I became more curious.

To survive the harshness of the wasteland, you must use cindermint, an in-game resource gained for surviving turns and killing enemies, to spawn defenders, with three base classes to choose from. The revolver-wielding Gunslinger is your primary damage dealer, while the Radshot applies corrosive radiation damage, and the Nomad offers a close-range shotgun blast with knockback.

Those base-level characters offer solid variety upon which to build. And that’s where the main hook for Australia Did It comes in: experimentation through combination. In the midst of battle, you can merge two units of the same level to create new, more powerful defenders, influenced by the traits of those used in the merge. At the onset, you can merge two Nomads to create a level 2 Nomad with increased damage and knockback, but the real fun comes in combining disparate units to create completely new characters. Even now, more than 15 hours into my gameplay, I’m still concocting new combinations I want to try on my next run.

By the end of my first successful run, I had multiple level 6 characters, including a railgun-toting heavy, mages who steal health from enemies and redistribute it to nearby allies, a drone that can move beyond the walls of the station to attack enemies directly, and, my personal favorite, a dual-shotgun-wielding one-man wrecking crew. However, many of these higher-level units also possess drawbacks to consider, like the railgun scorching all adjacent tiles or the drone running out of battery if it’s outside the walls for too long. Though I started keeping notes in my head about which combinations led to my favorite results, I was grateful for a comprehensive compendium that tracked the tens of unit types I unlocked through this rewarding experimentation.

The meat of the experience places your squad on a 25-tile square board with enemies spawning from the four principal directions. Thoughtfulness and positioning are crucial, as each unit on your squad possesses different traits and movement efficiency, as do the encroaching enemies. Basic enemies often make a beeline toward the station, while others may take a weaving route or keep their distance and blast you at range. Improvising and adjusting your strategy on the fly is the most engaging part of Australia Did It, and when you perfectly adapt in the moment, or escape the scenario by the skin of your teeth, there are few better feelings I’ve experienced in a game this year.

Your goal in this phase is to simply defend the station and gather resources to strengthen your squad before evacuating and moving on to the next area. Considering each unit's strengths, weaknesses, and capabilities while strategically positioning them around the station takes some getting used to, especially during the more chaotic stages. I fist-pumped as I watched the train pull out of a station that was about to crumble, and I lamented the loss of high-level units I had to leave behind to ensure the survival of the convoy. The process is ceaselessly thrilling, even as you begin to see how the gears work under the hood. I just wish I could say the same about the intervening train sections.

Once you escape the turn-based strategy portion, your surviving squad members hop aboard the train and chart their route. Using a basic map, you choose your next stop, with factors like enemy types and modifiers shown to you ahead of time. The top-down train segments between station-defense stages are largely passive; the units you evacuated from the previous station automatically attack swarming enemies with the same traits and perks they have in the main gameplay areas. You can aim a focus cone to instruct your units, but you’re at the mercy of the units you’ve brought. You can trigger an ultimate ability to send your defenders into overdrive, but I rarely needed it.

While I love the idea of intentionally crafting a team that’s good at both the turn-based strategy and bullet-heaven transport sections, I was never fully engaged getting from point A to point B. Instead, I often caught myself checking how much longer before my train arrived at the next station; these sections can be completed in a minute or two, but that doesn’t alleviate the feeling that it’s a step down from the other gameplay. These novel portions aren’t bad by any means; they’re merely an average part of an otherwise excellent experience.

Looking back on the hours I poured into Australia Did It, the forgettable train segments will occupy only a small part of my memories, just as they do in each run. Instead, what will stick with me for months to come are the creative combination mechanics, the outstanding turn-based defense system, and the thrill of uncovering the mysteries of this bleak, yet engaging world.

#4194. Company of Heroes 3: Operation Torch Review

Company of Heroes 3: Operation Torch delivers a replayable North African campaign with strong mission design, despite minor frustrations.

Company of Heroes 3 has come a long way since its 2023 release, slowly making its way to the real-time strategy hall of fame after a rather rough start. And yet, until now, something was missing.

Update 3.0 helped bring the game to its full potential, but mechanical polish only goes so far. Until recently, Company of Heroes 3 was a brilliant strategy game with strong mechanics that lend themselves well to single-player, but this was offset by a lack of quality content you could go through solo.

The dynamic campaign remains the highlight of Company of Heroes 3, but thanks to Operation Torch, the game finally has a scripted, story campaign that’s worth the trouble.

Operation Torch is the first single-player campaign DLC for Company of Heroes 3. It was preceded by the unorthodox yet highly entertaining Final Stand tower defence DLC, but surviving wave after wave of German tanks is no substitute for a touching story.

In that sense, the choice to depict Operation Torch is a poetic one. While American forces were being put through wringer in Pacific islands, the US had yet to launch any major land operations against the Germans and Italians.

Frontier Developments returns to the animal park with Planet Zoo 2.

The North Africa landings sent a green Army against veteran enemies. The Americans turned out to be quite adept at learning on the job, but the lessons there were written in blood. As a DLC, Operation Torch is similar.

Company of Heroes 3 emerges victorious once you see it through, but that success comes on the back of some blunders and failures that I hope are not repeated if or when Relic Entertainment decides another story-driven DLC is due.

The DLC focuses on three American soldiers from the US Army’s 34th Infantry Division, all the way from the landings in Algeria to the crushing of Axis resistance in Tunisia.

As far as individual story beats go, Operation Torch is adequate. Becker, Russo and Flanagan are likeable and quite distinct, and their commentary enhances the missions for the most part. There are some occasional immersion-breaking bits that strike out as silly, just about all of them relating to ‘tutorial’ speech.

For example, in a rather late mission in the campaign, Becker instructs us to defend fuel points because “we need the fuel to build tanks.” Well yes, Colonel, in game we do, but I’m operating under the assumption that these tanks were manufactured in a plant somewhere in Detroit rather than spontaneously spawned through good vibes and virtual resources somewhere in Tunisia.

This is nowhere near as egregious as in the much-maligned Rommel campaign that comes with the base game, but it would have been nice to have the option to disable tutorial-style objectives and commentary for people who are familiar with the game or who are going for a second playthrough.

I need to emphasize repeat playthroughs here because, although Operation Torch is a linear, story-based DLC, it incorporates lessons from other Company of Heroes 3 releases that make it more replayable than other campaigns in a similar vein.

Most missions are fairly open-ended in terms of how you can approach them. This is complemented by a decent degree of customization after each mission depending on how you accomplish both primary and secondary objectives. The Italy campaign had similar choices, but the Operation Torch system is closer to that of the Final Stand DLC.

The effects of the upgrades you pick are rather tangible. For example, early on, I managed to unlock M3 assault halftracks as a command call-in. Despite being rather underwhelming in their basic battle taxi configuration, these can be converted into game-changers.

The Americans turned out to be quite adept at learning on the job, but the lessons there were written in blood.

Many of my missions were saved because I was able to bring in an M3 converted into 75mm gun carriers that provided quick, on-call artillery support to break down defenses. When dug in myself, the M16 variant with the .50 quad-mounts made mince out of Axis infantry, allowing outnumbered defenders to hold out. All of this could have gone differently had I chosen another upgrade perk, which would have had its own advantages.

Final Stand’s influence is particularly felt in those defensive scenarios, where its wave mechanics reach their zenith.

Base game mechanics sometimes make these last stands slightly less dramatic than they could be at first, primarily because, as in real life, liberal application of engineering obstacles and overlapping fields of fire make incoming waves trivial. That false sense of safety comes apart spectacularly once heavier armor rolls in and you learn that Bazookas can’t dent it.

Relic managed to craft missions that reward sound tactics. Generally speaking, if it works in real life, it will work here. There is one exception that deserves its own section, and that’s the abysmal commando raid mission.

When the Operation Torch announcement came about late last month, the commando gameplay was by far the most exciting part. I’ve been counting the days until SAS: Rogue Heroes comes back for its third season, and I was hoping the commando levels would be a good way to make the wait easier. I was sorely mistaken, I’m afraid.

The level where you plant explosive charges is an affront to modern game design, primarily because it is just… Pac-Man. With guns.

You play one lonely commando, and your job is to slip by German patrols to plant demolition charges on 88mm guns. Every time you die (which, in my experience, is a lot), you respawn on the last checkpoint. Besides snipers, taking out any enemy does virtually nothing as they respawn almost immediately as well.

The result is a level that’s both archaic and devoid of meaning. There’s no way to fail the mission, as you just keep sending more and more single commandos into the breech, the Germans reciprocate, and you’re sitting there playing Pac-Man timing patrol movement patterns for a dry 30 minutes.

The mission is a one off, much like the American debacle in the Kasserine Pass in February 1943, but it leaves a mark on what’s otherwise a well-built campaign with strong design and balancing.

Playing Operation Torch and the Italy campaign back-to-back has been great because you get to see how far Allied land operations in the Mediterranean Theater of Operations have come from the shaky landings in Algeria to the assault on Monte Cassino that opened the road to Rome.

It’s nice to see an oft-forgotten part of World War 2 history given the attention it deserves. The British and German versions of the fight for North Africa have been told a million times over, but with a few exceptions (most notably Call of Duty 2: Big Red One), the American African campaign is constantly overshadowed by later exploits in Europe and the Pacific.

Operation Torch also lays out a blueprint for potential future DLCs that focus on telling stories, rather than just adding new units to the same old multiplayer slog. The combined force of this DLC with update 3.0 released earlier this month puts Company of Heroes 3 in the spot it was always meant to occupy since its launch.

Relic made a bold choice in depicting Operation Torch to this degree, and it paid off in spades. Company of Heroes 3 mechanics come alive in a fight that doesn’t get the attention it deserves, in spite of occasional hiccups. The first narrative-driven DLC for the game shows that there’s plenty of untapped potential in it, and it’s left me hoping more of them will come.

#4193. QoR sweep Maryville to reach VCT Americas Kickoff North America playoffs after opening loss

QoR's 2-0 win over Maryville University completed a recovery from an opening defeat at the VCT Americas Kickoff North America qualifiers. A Kickoff place and a Red Bull Home Ground spot both stay within QoR's reach as a result.

The line-up of ExpMoe, calamity, vanitas, yearn and dynamic was one of eight teams Riot Games invited directly to the North America Qualifier Playoffs. Cloud9, ENVY and two Shopify Rebellion line-ups were also on that list.

Before facing Maryville, QoR edged Shopify Rebellion Gold 2-1 in round two. In the Swiss stage, two wins sent a team through and two losses knocked it out. QoR sit 99th in the Elo power rankings, with a rating of 1590 and a 37-34 record across 71 rated matches.

Maryville came through the second open qualifier, held from 12 to 15 November, which drew 512 teams. They finished in the top two of that bracket. They then opened this event by sweeping Shopify Rebellion Gold.

A 0-2 loss to Cloud9 followed, and defeat by QoR left them with two losses. In the other round-three matches, Oafs beat SaD Esports, counterfeit beat FlyQuest and Wildcard beat Winthrop, each without dropping a map. The Elo table places Maryville 161st, with a rating of 1521 and a 6-7 record in 13 rated matches.

The playoffs are an eight-team double-elimination bracket. The winner takes North America’s direct place at the 2027 VCT Americas Kickoff in São Paulo. The runner-up goes to the Americas Last Chance Qualifier, also in São Paulo, on 17 and 18 December. That event is the last route into Kickoff. Eight partner teams are invited to Kickoff, and four places go to non-partner teams.

Riot runs the North America qualifiers with Red Bull. They also serve as the North America qualifiers for Red Bull Home Ground. The Los Angeles event runs from 10 to 13 December. Ten teams will play for a total prize pool of $100,000 USD. Eight are invited from around the world, and two earn their places through regional qualifiers. Riot will also reveal the 2027 Kickoff draws live on stage there.

Fnatic are EMEA’s invited team. The organisation is rebuilding its roster after parting with several players, including long-serving captain Jake ‘Boaster’ Howlett, Red Bull said.

#4192. Nioh 3’s generous demo is out now, and your progress carries over to the full game

If you’re looking for a way to check out one of the biggest releases of early 2026, Team Ninja has made it easy for you.

Nioh 3 is one of the most anticipated games of 2026, and it’s easily among the biggest releases of February. We’re a few days away from the start of that month, however, but we don’t have to wait until then to actually play Team Ninja’s next major release.

The previously announced demo has arrived, and it’s one any fan of action games should check out, especially if you missed the PlayStation-exclusive beta held last year.

Unlike previous tests, the Nioh 3 demo is available on PC and PS5, just like the main game. This is pretty new for the series, which has typically launched first on PlayStation before coming to PC months later.

The Nioh 3 demo includes a decent portion of content from the beginning of the game. It’s enough to show off the core duality mechanic, letting you switch between the Samurai and Ninja styles at will. It also includes a preview of the game’s open field level design, which makes it sit somewhere between full open world and the more linear level design of past Nioh games.

Feedback from the previous beta has been implemented into the demo (and full release), so you may see some familiar faces, as well as areas you visited before - assuming you played that one.

Another big reason why you might want to grab the Nioh 3 demo is that your progress in it will carry over to the full version. This includes the character creator, too, meaning you can spend all day perfecting your character without having to worry about missing out on playing the actual game.

The demo even supports online multiplayer for up to three players, in case you come to Nioh for co-op. If you complete the available content, you’ll earn an in-game bonus in the full version. This is something Team Ninja has done with past Nioh titles, of course.

This time, your reward is the Twin-Snake Helmet. Just make sure you complete the demo before February 15.

Nioh 3 is out February 6 on PC, and PlayStation 5.

#4191. Bandai Namco Shuts Down Unknown 9: Awakening Developer Reflector Entertainment

Bandai Namco has announced it is shutting down Reflector Entertainment, the Montreal studio behind 2024’s Unknown 9: Awakening.

Reflector, founded in 2015, is a subsidiary of Bandai Namco that was acquired in 2020. Unknown 9: Awakening is the studio’s only released title, which was first revealed at Gamescom 2020 and released on October 17, 2024. The third-person action game is set within the broader Unknown 9 transmedia franchise, which includes a book trilogy, comics, and a web series, and stars Haroona, a woman able to traverse a separate dimension called the Fold. Haroona, played by The Witcher actress Anya Chalotra, uses this ability and other supernatural powers to battle a hostile secret society across India and other global locations.

Upon release, Unknown 9: Awakening didn’t make much of a critical splash; it currently has a 59 Metascore and "Mixed" Steam reviews. In November 2024, a month after Unknown 9's launch, Reflector laid off 18 percent of its staff.  More layoffs were announced in January 2025 as Reflector canned an unannounced project while confirming Unknown 9 failed to meet expectations. With Reflector’s dissolution, Bandai Namco expects to post “an extraordinary loss” of approximately €21 million on its Q3 financial results for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027.

#4189. PlayStation Cancels In-Development Live-Service Shooter, Fairgames, At Jade Raymond's Former Haven Studio

PlayStation has reportedly canceled Fairgames, the long-in-development live-service shooter being made by Haven Studios, which Jade Raymond founded in 2021. Sony acquired Haven in 2022, and in 2025, Raymond left the studio, though it remained dedicated to developing Fairgames without her. It seems the story of Fairgames is now over, according to a new Bloomberg report.

The publication reports that PlayStation will not enforce any job cuts or layoffs as a result of Fairgames' cancellation, which comes as a surprise, and the studio will instead shift to support other first-party teams under the PlayStation umbrella. According to Bloomberg, this cancellation comes after a recent test of the game that allowed "thousands of players" to check it out did not deliver the results PlayStation wanted.

"While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set," PlayStation executives Sean Decker and John Doyle wrote in an email to employees today, according to Bloomberg. "Combined with challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre, we have made the difficult decision to cease development on the game."

This doesn't necessarily come as a surprise. PlayStation announced Fairgames back in 2023 and hasn't shown much since, leaving many to assume development has been struggling behind the scenes. Since then, PlayStation has pulled back heavily on its live-service plans, which originally included launching more than 10 live-service games by March of this year. Naughty Dog's Last of Us multiplayer game was canceled, Bungie ended active development on Destiny 2, and live-service Horizon spin-off Hunters Gathering is reportedly being overhauled following poor playtest feedback, amongst other stories. Reading between the lines, many fans were waiting for news like today's cancellation of Fairgames to drop.

Still, in an era where games are canceled and entire teams are laid off (sometimes even after releasing a successful game), it's nice to see Haven employees are not facing layoffs.

#4187. Quantic Dream addresses toxicity, tech bugs and tutorials for Spellcasters Chronicles closed beta 2 - here's how to get a key

Here are the start and end times for the second Spellcasters Chronicles closed beta, as well as what's new in this latest test.

Quantic Dream has opened up its upcoming fantasy MOBA for a second closed beta weekend starting from today, January 29, until 9AM UTC on Monday February 2.

The closed beta is for PC only in Europe, Asia and North America and potential players can register to join the waitlist for a key at the game’s official website or on the Spellcasters Chronicles Steam page. Players who had access to the first closed beta will automatically have access to the second, but you can sign up on both the site and Steam to increase your chances of entry.

The MOBA genre is competitive in every sense and Quantic Dream is trying to break into it with a Magic the Gathering-esque spin on the format. Players build a deck of cards before queuing into teams of 3, then face off as battling mages, summoning creatures, building fortifications and casting spells rather than choosing a Hero with unique abilities in the traditional MOBA style.

Beta content includes a new map, 6 new spells and 5 new summon creatures for your deck, as well as 3 new buildings too.
